list.listitem: Suspect oropharyngeal or esophageal candidiasis in at-risk patients with pain or discomfort in the mouth, angles of the lips, or beneath an oral prosthesis; or who have dysphagia or chest pain when swallowing. C
Visually examine the oropharynx; scrape lesions and examine with KOH or Gram stain, if necessary, to confirm the diagnosis. C
If the history and scrapings are consistent with oropharyngeal candidiasis, begin therapy with fluconazole for 7 to 14 days. A

Treat mild oropharyngeal candidiasis (OPC) with clotrimazole troche or miconazole mucoadhesive buccal tablet, and moderate to severe disease with oral fluconazole 100 to 200 mg daily for 7 to 14 das. A

For esophageal candidiasis, IDSA guidelines (2016) recommend oral fluconazole 200 to 400 mg daily for 14 to 21 days. If patients can't tolerate oral therapy, IV fluconazole 6 mg/kg daily (400 mg) or either micafungin 150 mg daily, caspofungin (70 mg load then 50 mg per day), or anidulafungin 200 mg daily are alternatives. A
If candidemia accompanies esophageal or pharyngeal disease, an intravenous antifungal preparation should be used chosen according to Candida species and probable or known susceptibility. C

background.definition: Mucosal infection of one or more anatomical sites: the buccal cavity, tongue surface, lip margins (angular cheilitis) and/or distal esophagus with Candida species. Candida species are strictly opportunistic pathogens. This implies a disturbance of innate or acquired immunity at the mucosal surface in the host. The fungus happens to be present and takes advantage of the dysbiotic circumstances.

list.listitem: In one study, 56% of patients with HIV had at least one episode of oropharyngeal candidiasis prior to therapy with protease inhibitors for HIV, compared to 9% after therapy was initiated.
In a series of 18 patients treated with beclomethasone 672 mcg/day via MDI, 4 had oropharyngeal candidiasis and 12 were colonized.

In a French study of 2042 patients with cancer (solid tumor and/or lymphoma) treated with chemotherapy and/or radiotherapy, 9.6% (95% CI, 8.4%-11%) had oropharyngeal candidiasis. Oropharyngeal candidiasis was most frequent in patients treated with combined chemoradiotherapy (22.0%) or with more than 2 cytotoxic agents (16.9%).
In a systematic review, the weighted prevalence of clinical oral fungal infection was found to be 7.5% pretreatment, 39.1% during treatment, and 32.6% after the end of cancer therapy.
The most common cause of mucous membrane candidiasis is Candida albicans.
C. dubliniensis causes the same process in many HIV-infected individuals.
Other non-albicans species can infrequently be the cause of oropharyngeal candidiasis.
In patients refractory to OPC therapy, consider a non-albicans species; culture the oropharynx and confirm.

OPC is seen most frequently in HIV-infected patients, associated with a reduction in cell-mediated immunity. Oropharyngeal candidiasis is the most common opportunistic infection in individuals with HIV-1 infection, usually in patients with <200 CD4 cells/μL. Other predisposing factors include: oral steroid inhalers, denture wear, broad-spectrum antibiotic use and diabetes mellitus. Oropharyngeal candidiasis is seen often in neutropenic patients and those with post chemotherapy mucositis.

Uncommonly, in the absence of such risk factors discussed above, chronic, recurrent mucocutaneous candidiasis (CMC) is seen with a genetic disorder, Autoimmune Polyendrinopathy-Candidasis-Ectodermal Dystrophy (a mutation in the AIRE gene) and other endocrinopathies of unknown causation. Therapies that target IL-17R such as brodalumab for psoriasis increase the risk for OPC.

Esophageal candidiasis occurs in 2 settings: patients with AIDS and CD4+ cell counts below 100 cells/μL ( the fungi do not invade the muscularis laye r), and in neutropenic patients (carries a risk for mucosal invasion and vascular dissemination of the fungus; this is a grave medical emergency).
Candida species express cell surface amyloid that leads to host deposition of serum amyloid P component; this protein may dampen the host response to the pathogen.
Candida albicans possesses a complex network of genes that may assist in colonizing or invading exposed tissue in the mammalian host.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Prolonged steroids and antibiotics for hospitalized/ventilated patients with COVID-19
IL-17 inhibitors for psoriasis, psoriatic arthritis and ankylosing spondylitis (weakens mucosal immunity)
Reduced cell mediated immunity (due to HIV)
Oral steroid inhalers (probably depresses local cell-mediated immunity)
Denture wear (occurs beneath the plate; often with intense erythema)
Malfitting dentures (causes cheilitis at the angles of the mouth)
Broad spectrum antibiotics (eliminate competing microbes in mucosal niches)
Genetic disorders such as chronic granulomatous disease and chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis (consider if candidiasis is refractory, recurrent, or destructive)

list.listitem: Patients receiving cancer chemotherapy should receive prophylaxis for oropharyngeal candidiasis: prescribe an oral absorbable azole; fluconazole is effective for almost all patients. A In a systematic review, prophylactic use of fluconazole during cancer therapy resulted in a 1.9% prevalence of clinical fungal infection. Nystatin was not found to be effective in a Cochrane review of immunosuppressed patients.

Prevention of oropharyngeal candidiasis in patients with HIV has not been well studied but fluconazole and clotrimazole appear to be effective. Following implementation of antiretroviral therapy, the incidence of oropharyngeal candidiasis declines even without use of antifungals. Itraconazole and ketoconazole should be avoided in patients receiving protease inhibitors. B

In select patient groups (eg, hematopoetic stem cell transplantation and bone marrow transplants), posaconazole may be the drug of choice to prevent oropharyngeal candidiasis since it has broad activity against filamentous fungi which may cause invasive diseases in these hosts. C
For high-risk adult ICU patients, consider fluconazole or alternatively caspofungin, anidulafungin, or micafungin to prevent candidiasis. B

Suspect oropharyngeal or esophageal candidiasis in at-risk patients with pain or discomfort in the mouth, angles of the lips, or beneath an oral prosthesis; or who have dysphagia or chest pain when swallowing. C
Visually examine the oropharynx and scrape lesions if necessary to confirm the diagnosis. C

Examine scrapings with KOH or Gram stain for typical fungal elements. This is done for confirmation of the clinical impression—many oral lesions look like candidiasis but lack microscopic evidence of the fungi. C
Examine biopsies or brushings of esophageal lesions for typical fungal elements (yeast cells and filamentous forms). C

Differential.Differential_Features: Greyish, membranous growth on mucosa that is striated; caused by Epstein-Barr virus
Can be white in color; caused by elongation of the filiform papillae

list.listitem: The diagnosis of oropharyngeal candidiasis is suggested by typical symptoms of pain or discomfort in the mouth, angles of the lips, or beneath an oral prosthesis.
The diagnosis of esophageal candidiasis is suggested by typical symptoms of pain in the chest with swallowing or difficulty swallowing liquids or solids.

Both of the above diagnoses are found in at-risk patients listed above, including HIV-positive individuals, neutropenic patients, patients using steroid inhalers or oral prostheses, and occasionally in very young children on broad-spectrum antibiotics.

The diagnosis is made by direct visualization, looking into the oropharynx or use of an endoscope to demonstrate the typical pseudomembranes; this can be confirmed by Gram stain or potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation of a scraping, brushing or biopsy in the case of esophagitis. A trial of therapy is often warranted in patients with presumed esophageal candidiasis before resorting to endoscopy.

Not all oropharyngeal candidiasis will present with pseudomembranes. Erythematous oral candidiasis is intensely red and is accompanied by pain and discomfort; it occurs often beneath dentures. There are no pseudomembranes in this presentation. This variety can be suspected because it occurs in patients at risk (see above).

Scrapings of lesions of oropharyngeal candidiasis are observed under the microscope with either 10% potassium hydroxide (KOH) or Gram stain (requires more time and more reagents than KOH). Findings on microscopy confirm the visual impression of oropharyngeal candidiasis lesions: yeast cells and filamentous forms of the fungus are usually seen in abundance along with adherent oral bacteria and occasional polymorphonuclear leukocytes, all on an eosinophilic background.

Biopsy specimens of esophageal pseudomembranes demonstrate fungal elements on the mucosa (in the case of HIV-infected patients) or invading the muscularis (in the case of neutropenic patients). Patients with esophageal candidiasis may or may not have simultaneous oropharyngeal candidiasis.

IDSA guidelines (2016) recommend testing for azole susceptibility in all patients with candidemia. Patients with candidemia should have follow-up blood cultures daily to determine when candidemia has resolved.

Suspect oropharyngeal candidiasis or esophageal candidiasis in at-risk patients with pain or discomfort in the mouth, angles of the lips, or beneath an oral prosthesis; or pain perceived in the chest when swallowing liquids or solids.
Inspect the oropharynx or visualize the distal esophagus by endoscopy. Pseudomembranes can be scraped in the case of OPC and biopsied in Candida esophagitis.
Gram stain of OPC scrapings will confirm the diagnosis as will histological examination of esophageal lesions.
Consider a trial of therapy in patients with presumed esophageal candidiasis before resorting to endoscopy.
Treat mild OPC with clotrimazole troche or miconazole mucoadhesive buccal tablet, and moderate to severe disease with oral fluconazole 100 to 200 mg daily for 7 to 14 days. A

For esophageal candidiasis, IDSA guidelines (2016) recommend oral fluconazole 200 to 400 mg daily for 14 to 21 days. If patients can't tolerate oral therapy, IV fluconazole 6 mg/kg daily (400 mg) or either micafungin 150 mg daily, caspofungin (70 mg load then 50 mg per day), or anidulafungin 200 mg daily are alternatives. A
If candidemia accompanies esophageal or pharyngeal disease, an intravenous antifungal preparation should be used chosen according to Candida species and probable or known susceptibility. C
Drugs for treatment of oropharyngeal and esophageal candidiasis are shown in .

Treat mild OPC with clotrimazole troche 10 mg 5 times daily or miconazole mucoadhesive buccal 50 mg tablet that is applied to the mucosa over the canine fossa once daily for 7 to 14 days. Nystatin suspension or pastilles are alternatives.
For patients with moderate to severe oropharyngeal disease, oral fluconazole 100-200 mg daily for 7 to 14 days is recommended by IDSA 2016 guidelines.

For patients who don't respond to fluconazole, itraconazole solution 200 mg once daily or posaconazole suspension 400 mg twice daily for 3 days and then 400 mg daily are recommended for up to 4 weeks. Voriconazole 200 mg twice daily is an alternative for fluconazole-refractory infection.
Another alternative for patients with disease non-responsive to fluconazole is IV caspofungin 70 mg load and then 50 mg daily, or micafungin 100 mg daily.
Gentian violet and lemon juice may be adequate for HIV-infected patients with OPC in resource-poor settings.

IDSA guidelines (2016) recommend oral fluconazole 200 to 400 mg daily for 14 to 21 days. If patients can't tolerate oral therapy, IV fluconazole 6 mg/kg daily (400 mg) or either micafungin 150 mg daily, caspofungin (70 mg load then 50 mg per day), or anidulafungin 200 mg daily are alternatives.
Once patients can tolerate oral therapy, switch to fluconazole 200 to 400 mg daily.
For patients with disease not responding to fluconazole, use itraconazole solution 200 mg daily or voriconazole 200 mg twice daily either IV or orally for 2 to 3 weeks.
If candidemia accompanies esophageal or pharyngeal disease, an intravenous antifungal preparation should be used chosen according to Candida species and probable or known susceptibility. C
In an RCT of 50 patients with primarily Candida denture stomatitis, 2% uncaria tomentosa (cat's claw) performed as well as 2% miconazole in reducing colony counts.

In a systematic review of 15 studies, antimicrobial photodynamic therapy using primarily methylene blue, toluidine blue, or porphyrin derivative as photosensitizers was effective in treating oral fungal infections.

Inclusion of local probiotics to 2% nystatin paste vs. nystatin paste alone in an RCT of 65 patients with Candida-associated stomatitis reduced detection rate of Candida species but did not result in differences in clinical improvement.
Oropharyngeal candidiasis: 7 to 14 days
Esophageal candidiasis: 14 to 21 days
Patients with esophageal candidiasis and neutropenia should be hospitalized.

Many patients with AIDS and symptoms of esophageal candidiasis can be empirically treated as outpatients for candidiasis provided they can swallow pills and are not obstructed. If there is no improvement, esophagoscopy should be performed.
Prognosis is excellent and treatment is effective in the great majority of cases.
Problem may recur if the underlying problem continues; for example, CD4 cell count below 100 cells/mm3 or neutropenia recurs.
Untreated OPC in HIV-infected individuals can become chronic forming a leathery pseudomembrane over the soft palate.
Untreated esophageal candidiasis in HIV-infected individuals may lead to occlusion of the esophagus by pseudomembrane formation leading to inanition.
Untreated esophageal candidiasis in neutropenic patients can lead to invasion of the muscularis with resultant candidemia or esophageal rupture.
In the typical case of OPC, lesions will disappear within 1 to 2 days of beginning appropriate oral therapy. The therapy should be continued for 7 to 14 days.

Esophageal candidiasis is often treated with intravenous antifungals, either an azole such as fluconazole or an echinocandin. The disease rapidly responds to amphotericin-B as well. The treatment duration is more prolonged (14-21 days).
Repeat endoscopy to follow esophageal lesions is not needed if the patient responds to therapy.

Denture stomatitis is common in older populations. Removal of the prosthesis is required to reveal the inflamed mucosa. Adequate and frequent cleaning of the prosthesis should be performed as well as oral azole therapy and this alone may be sufficient.
Absorbable azoles are not recommended in pregnancy.
Localized infections, such as OPC, can be treated with a nonabsorbable azole such as clotrimazole troches or a polyene that is not systemically absorbed such as nystatin.
Nonabsorbable azoles or polyenes are preferred for treatment of OPC in children.
Candida esophagitis should be treated with an intravenous echinocandin or amphotericin-B.

feature.caption: Oral Antifungal Agents for the Treatment of Oropharyngeal Candidiasis and IV Agents for Esophageal Candidiasis.
feature.feature_body:
Antifungal Agent Dosage Comment
Oropharyngeal Candidiasis
Clotrimazole troches 10 mg 5 times per day for 14 days For mild disease only. Requires multiple doses/day; patient acceptance is sometimes a problem; a topical drug is not as effective as orally absorbed drug
Miconazole mucoadhesive tablet Applied once daily for 7-14 days For mild disease only.
Fluconazole 100 mg -200 mg daily for 7-14 days For moderate to severe disease. Highly effective, inexpensive, has few adverse effects, is given once a day; drug interactions through CYP-450 enzyme system with antiretroviral therapy are not a problem
IV form available
Rectal form available
Itraconazole 200 mg per day for 14 days For fluconazole refractory disease. Effective but has significant “bidirectional” interactions through the CYP-450 enzyme system with antiretroviral therapy; expensive; absorption may be a problem as an acid pH in the stomach must be present .
IV form available
Nystatin suspension 400,000-600,000 U 4 times per day for 14 days Alternative for mild disease. Relatively expensive and requires multiple doses/day; dysgeusia limits acceptance; it is a topical drug and not as effective as an orally absorbed drug. Should not use with neutropenic patients or those receiving chemotherapy as it is ineffective in these populations
Posaconazole Loading dose of 100 mg twice daily on first day, then 100 mg once daily for 13 days For fluconazole refractory disease. Effective, expensive; CYP-450 interactions are minor; broad antifungal spectrum used as prophylaxis for filamentous fungi in at-risk patients . Probably should be the azole of choice in bone marrow transplant and hematopoetic stem cell transplant patients due to infections with Aspergillus and Mucorales species
Voriconazole 200 mg every 12 h for 14 days Effective but has significant “bidirectional” interactions through the CYP-450 enzyme system with antiretroviral therapy
IV form available
Caspofungin, anidulafungin or micafungin Caspafungin: 70 mg loading dose followed by 50 mg a day Micafungin: 150 mg once dailyAnidulafungin: 200 mg once daily Alternative for moderate to severe disease. Very expensive.
Esophageal Candidiasis
Fluconazole 200 to 400 mg (3 - 6 mg/kg) once a day Initial drug of choice. Mild to moderate cases can be treated with oral drug; those begun on intravenous drug can usually be switched to oral drug after improvement
Caspofungin, anidulafungin or micafungin Caspafungin: 70 mg loading dose followed by 50 mg a day Micafungin: 150 mg once dailyAnidulafungin: 200 mg once daily Expensive , for patients who cannot tolerate oral therapy.
Amphotericin B (formulations with and without lipids) Depending on presentation, 0.4 to 1.0 mg/kg/d Highly effective; may reduce kidney function in non-lipid formulations
Posaconazole Suspension 400 mg twice daily or extended release tablets 300 mg once daily For fluconazole refractory disease only.
Adapted from Klotz SA. Oropharyngeal candidiasis: a new treatment option. Clin Infect Dis 2006;42:1187-1188.
